subject: testing the effects of a predictor on RESIDUAL variance in CFA

messages.author: 2060c8e54fb73471
messages.subject: testing the effects of a predictor on RESIDUAL variance in CFA
parts:
Hello!

I have a 2nd order CFA model: one general factor G and four domain factors v, c, m and s.
I am trying to introduce an observed variable as a predictor, "RW". I want to find out if RW has an effect on any of the domain factors and/ or on G. 

1) First I modelled each factor separately and regressed it on RW. (which worked)

2) Second, I modelled G (with a second order model) and regressed only G on RW. (which again, I was able to do)

3) Now, I would like to test if, on top of its effect on G, RW also has an effect on the variance of the some domain factors which is not explained by G 

These would be my latent variables
 v =~ x1 + x2 + x3
 c =~ x4 + x5 + x6
 m =~ x7 + x8 + x9
 s =~ x10 + x11 + x12

 G =~ v + c + m + s

# and this is how I tried to model my "question number three":
G + m + s ~ RW

But it seems that all I did was control for the effect of RW on the domain factors BEFORE esitmating G, which is not what I meant. What I wanted to do was estimate G 
and THEN regress the residual 1st order factor variances on RW, but I don't know how to specify it, or if it is possible/advisable at all. Can anyone help me out, please?


P.S. I am going to try using a bifactor model instead of a hierarchical model, but I would still like to understand how to do this regression in a hierarchical model, in order to compare the results

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: testing the effects of a predictor on RESIDUAL variance in CFA
parts:
Federica--
     In most factor-based SEM estimation methods, there is no "before" or "after." Estimation is simultaneous, though there may be many rounds or iterations to obtain final estimates. Typically, that is seen as a virtue because it produces greater statistical efficiency.
     You describe estimating a model where RW predicts v, c, m, s, and then a second model where higher order factor G predicts the same common factors. If RW does predict the four factors, that would explain why a higher order factor works. G is a "latent variable" meaning that it stands for some influence not directly observeable in that model. But once you include RW as a predictor of the four factors, then the variable is no longer "latent," so there is nothing for G to represent.
     In the model where RW predicts indirectly through G, is the path between RW and G strong? That suggests that G is redundant, once RW is present.
     Another way to check this is to look at the model with RW but without G. If there is anything for G to represent, then it would be evident in the residual covariances of v, c, m, s.

v =~ x1 + x2 + x3
 c =~ x4 + x5 + x6
 m =~ x7 + x8 + x9
 s =~ x10 + x11 + x12

v+c+m+s ~ RW

v+c+m ~~ s
v+c ~~ m
v ~~ c

If those covariances are near 0, then there is no room for a higher order factor, once RW is present.

     Of course, we cannot say for certain that G and RW are redundant, even if their correlation is strong. But you may need some other variable in the model that can better distinguish the two.
--ED Rigdon

parts:
Hi Edward,

thank you for your answer.

I am findind it hard to apply it to my case, so I think it would be useful if I gave a little more context. This is a simplified version of my model. I am modelling cognitive functioning: visuospatial, crystallised, memory and processing speed factors + the second-order factor G. RW is a measure of education in adulthood. 

RW has weak but significant associations (between 0.2, and 0.3) with two of the four factors (visuospatial and crystallised) and with G as a whole. The loadings of the four factors on G are much stronger than their associations with RW. Therefore, I think I should be able to say that G is not redundant, right?

The question I am trying to answer now is if RW, besides being associated with general cognitive functioning (G) also has additional associations with specific cognitive abilities (e.g. visuospatial abilities) -- over and above its association with G

So, in the case where I have
G =~ v + c + m + s
is it possible to model a regression between e.g. the UNIQUE variance of v and RW (v ~ RW), in which the dependent variable is the variance of v not shared with G?

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: testing the effects of a predictor on RESIDUAL variance in CFA
parts:
Federica--
     That additional information is very helpful.  There are a couple of ways to do this. The simplest is to add direct paths from RW to the individual facets along with the higher order G factor. If covariance between G and RW is not too high, then collinearity won't be much of a problem.
     A somewhat more complex approach is to replace the error variances / residual variances for the facets with new common factors, and then let RW predict those. This involves these steps:

1. Create one new factor for each of the four facets and standardize it (to solve the identification problem). You can do that via

v_res + c_res + m_res + s_res =~ 0*x1
v_res ~~ 1 * v_res                                       #one for v, c, m, s

(The operator =~ tells lavaan to create new common factors...it doesn't matter which observed variables appear on the right hand side, as long as the loading is fixed to 0.)

2. Add the relevant "residual" term to the equation for the facet, e.g.:

v ~ v_res

(along with the higher order factor statement C =~ v + c + m + s)

3. Fix the residual variances of v, c, m, s to 0:

v ~~ 0 * v                        # one each for v, c, m, s

You may need to provide a starting value for the path between facet and "residual factor." Take the square root of the residual variance reported in a regular analysis.

4. Add the paths for RW predicting these "residua variances":

v_res + c_res + m_res + s_res ~ RW 

Make sure that RW is not predicting the facets v, c, m, s at the same time.

This should work. You probably want to try it adding one facet at a time.

--Ed Rigdon
